title: Heap index arithmetic
prompt: A heap is stored in an array. Fill in the index formulas for node `i` (0-based).
code:
int left   = {{1}};   // left child of i
int right  = {{2}};   // right child of i
int parent = {{3}};   // parent of i (i > 0)
explanation: Level-order packing puts node i's children at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and integer division makes (i-1)/2 the parent for both of them. Because a heap of n elements is only about log₂ n levels deep, sifting an element up (offer) or down (poll) takes O(log n) swaps.

title: Poll order
prompt: Offer 4, 1, 7, 3 into a default `PriorityQueue<Integer>`, then poll twice. What comes out?
explanation: Default PriorityQueue is a min-heap: poll always returns the minimum of what's inside right now.

title: Build a max-heap of pairs
prompt: Order `int[]{value, index}` pairs so the LARGEST value polls first.
code: PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare({{1}}[0], {{2}}[0]));
explanation: `Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])` sorts ascending (min-heap); swapping to `(b[0], a[0])` reverses it. Prefer `Integer.compare` over `b[0] - a[0]`, which can overflow.

title: K-th largest element
prompt: Return the k-th largest element of `nums` using the size-k min-heap pattern (offer everything, poll when size exceeds k, answer is `peek`).

solution.explanation: O(n log k) — better than sorting when k is small. The heap holds exactly the k largest seen; its minimum is the k-th largest.

hints: Min-heap, cap at size k, evict with poll.
After the loop, `heap.peek()` is the answer.

title: Drill: k smallest, sorted
prompt: From memory: return the k smallest values of `nums` in ascending order. Offer everything into a min-heap, then poll k times into the result array. (Different from top-K: here the heap does the sorting.)

solution.explanation: Each `poll` returns the current minimum, so k polls produce the k smallest in ascending order. O(n log n) to fill the heap plus O(k log n) to drain.

hints: Let the heap do the sorting: put everything in, and the smallest comes out first every time.
Offer all n values, then `poll()` exactly k times into `res[i]`.

title: Recall: min-heap
prompt: Fill in the min-heap construction and operations.
code:
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new {{1}}<>();  // min-heap by default
pq.{{2}}(5);          // add
int min = pq.{{3}}(); // smallest, without removing
pq.{{4}}();           // remove the smallest
explanation: A default `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap; `offer` adds, `peek` reads the smallest, `poll` removes it.

title: Drill: min via heap
prompt: From memory: offer every element of `nums` (non-empty) into a min-heap and return the minimum with `peek`.

solution.explanation: A min-heap keeps its minimum at the root, so `peek` reads it in O(1) after n O(log n) offers.

hints: A default PriorityQueue keeps its smallest element at the front.

title: Recall: max-heap comparator
prompt: Complete the comparator that turns a PriorityQueue into a max-heap.
code:
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap =
    new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.{{1}}({{2}}, {{3}}));
explanation: `Integer.compare(b, a)` reverses the natural order, making the largest element poll first.

title: Drill: max via heap
prompt: From memory: return the maximum of `nums` (non-empty) using a MAX-heap (comparator `(a, b) -> Integer.compare(b, a)`), offering all and peeking.

solution.explanation: Reversing the comparator makes the largest value rank "smallest", so it sits at the root and `peek` returns the maximum. `Integer.compare(b, a)` avoids the overflow of `b - a`.

hints: A max-heap is a min-heap with the comparison flipped.
`new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(b, a))`, offer all, then `peek()`.
